t: ₹20,000 is invested for 4 years at 5% per annum. Compared with simple interest, how much MORE does compound interest produce? (1.05⁴ = 1.215506)
e: Compound amount = 20,000 × 1.215506 = ₹24,310; simple-interest amount = 20,000 × (1 + 0.20) = ₹24,000. The excess of ₹310 is the interest earned on interest.

t: A nominal rate of 12% per annum convertible monthly corresponds to an effective annual rate of approximately (1.01¹² = 1.126825)
e: Effective rate = (1 + 0.12/12)¹² − 1 = 1.126825 − 1 = 12.68%. Half-yearly conversion would give 12.36% and quarterly 12.55%.

t: ₹5,000 is paid at the end of each year for 3 years into an account earning 5% per annum. The accumulated value immediately after the last payment is (1.05² = 1.1025)
At 8% per annum (v = 0.92593, v² = 0.85734, v³ = 0.79383), the present value of an annuity-due of ₹1 per annum for 4 years is
e: ä₄ = 1 + v + v² + v³ = 1 + 0.92593 + 0.85734 + 0.79383 = 3.5771. The immediate annuity a₄ would be v × ä₄ = 3.3121.

t: For a positive rate of interest i, with d the rate of discount and δ the force of interest, the correct ordering is
e: Discount is deducted in advance so d < i, and the continuously compounded force lies between them: d < δ < i. For i = 5%: d = 4.76%, δ = 4.88%.

t: Given l₆₀ = 80,000, l₇₀ = 60,000 and l₈₀ = 30,000, the probability that a life aged 60 dies between ages 70 and 80 is
e: ₁₀|₁₀q₆₀ = (l₇₀ − l₈₀)/l₆₀ = 30,000/80,000 = 0.375. Dividing by l₇₀ instead gives ₁₀q₇₀ = 0.5, which is conditional on reaching 70.

t: If l₆₀ = 80,000 and l₆₂ = 78,300, the probability that a life aged 60 survives two years, ₂p₆₀, is
e: ₂p₆₀ = l₆₂/l₆₀ = 78,300/80,000 = 0.97875; the complement 0.02125 is ₂q₆₀.

t: ₹10,000 is invested at 6% per annum compound interest. What is the accumulated amount at the end of 2 years?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Accumulated value = 10,000 × (1.06)² = 10,000 × 1.1236 = ₹11,236. ₹11,200 is the simple-interest figure, which ignores interest on interest.

t: D₄₀ = 2,000 and D₄₁ = 1,880 at 5% interest. The one-year survival probability p₄₀ implied by these commutation values is
e: D₄₁/D₄₀ = v p₄₀ = 0.94, so p₄₀ = 0.94 × 1.05 = 0.987. The pure endowment factor contains both discount and survival.

t: If ä₆₅ = 10.2 at 5% interest (d = 0.047619), the whole life assurance factor A₆₅ is approximately
For (40): M₄₀ = 1,200, M₆₀ = 700, D₄₀ = 6,000, D₆₀ = 1,800. The net single premium for a 20-year endowment assurance of ₹3,00,000 is
A deferred annuity-due of ₹50,000 per annum commences at age 65 for a life now aged 55. With N₆₅ = 9,000 and D₅₅ = 1,500, the net single premium is
Compared with a whole life assurance with premiums payable throughout life, a whole life assurance with premiums limited to 20 years has, for the same age and sum assured,
e: The same benefit value must be met by fewer premiums (ä_{x:20} < ä_x), so each premium is larger; after year 20 the policy is fully paid and carries a substantial reserve.

t: A net premium of ₹8,000 is to be loaded for renewal expenses of 3% and profit of 5%, both expressed as percentages of the office premium. The office premium is approximately
e: P' = 8,000/(1 − 0.03 − 0.05) = 8,000/0.92 = ₹8,696. Adding 8% to the net premium (₹8,640) would understate the loading because it is defined on the office premium.

t: An agent earns 35% commission on the first year's premium and 5% on each renewal premium. On a 20-year policy with annual premium ₹10,000, the total commission over the term is
e: First-year commission 3,500 + 19 renewals × 500 = 9,500, total ₹13,000. The front-loaded structure is why initial expenses dominate the loading.

t: The net premium rate is 2.5% of sum assured, a policy fee of ₹500 per annum applies, and other expenses are 10% of the office premium. For a sum assured of ₹10,00,000 the office annual premium is
An endowment policy has reserve ₹50,000 at the start of the year before the premium of ₹6,000. Interest is 5%, q = 0.004 and sum assured ₹5,00,000. The reserve at the end of the year is approximately
If ä₃₀:₃₀ = 16 and ä₄₅:₁₅ = 10.4, the net premium reserve per ₹1 sum assured for a 30-year endowment on (30) after 15 years is
A paid-up policy has a paid-up sum assured of ₹1,20,000 and no further premiums are payable. If the appropriate assurance factor is 0.40, the reserve is
e: With no premiums to deduct, the prospective reserve = PV of benefits = 1,20,000 × 0.40 = ₹48,000.

t: If p₄₀ = 0.998 and p₃₅ = 0.999 for two independent lives, the probability that the joint life status (35, 40) survives one year is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). p_xy = p_x × p_y = 0.999 × 0.998 = 0.997002. The joint status fails on the first death, so both must survive.

t: A block of 1,000 policies each has sum at risk ₹5,00,000 and expected q = 0.005. Three deaths occur in the year. The mortality profit for the year is
e: Expected death strain = 1,000 × 0.005 × 5,00,000 = ₹25 lakh; actual = 3 × 5,00,000 = ₹15 lakh; profit = 25 − 15 = ₹10 lakh.

t: If the joint-life annuity-due ä_xy = 12 at a rate of discount d = 0.05, the value of a joint-life assurance of ₹1 payable on the first death, A_xy, is
e: A_xy = 1 − d ä_xy = 1 − 0.05 × 12 = 0.40, exactly as for a single life with the joint status replacing (x).

t: For independent lives with p_x = 0.9 and p_y = 0.8 over a year, the probability that exactly one of them survives the year is
e: P(exactly one) = p_x q_y + q_x p_y = 0.9 × 0.2 + 0.1 × 0.8 = 0.18 + 0.08 = 0.26. Both survive 0.72, neither 0.02.

t: In a select-and-ultimate table with a 2-year select period, which ordering of mortality rates for lives of the same attained age 42 is correct?
e: The most recently selected life has the lightest mortality: q_[42] < q_[41]+1 < q_42 (ultimate). Selection wears off over the select period.

t: Under a compound reversionary bonus of 4% per annum, a sum assured of ₹1,00,000 grows after 2 years to
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Compound bonus is declared on sum assured plus previously attached bonuses: 1,00,000 × 1.04² = ₹1,08,160. ₹1,08,000 is the simple-bonus figure.

t: An insurer cedes 50% of every policy under a quota share and then, on its retained share, cedes any amount above ₹20 lakh to a surplus treaty. For a policy of ₹1 crore the total amount reinsured is
e: Quota share cedes ₹50 lakh; of the retained ₹50 lakh, ₹30 lakh above the ₹20 lakh retention goes to the surplus treaty. Total ceded = 50 + 30 = ₹80 lakh; net retained ₹20 lakh.

t: A valuation data extract shows a policy with sum assured ₹1 crore and annual premium ₹500. The most likely reason this record is flagged is
o: sum assured exceeds the reinsurance retention
the plan is not in force
failure of a reasonableness check on the premium-to-sum-assured ratio
e: Reasonableness (ratio) checks compare premium with sum assured for the plan, age and term; a premium of ₹500 for ₹1 crore cover is implausible and indicates a data entry error.

t: A record in which the maturity date is earlier than the date of commencement would be detected by a
e: Logical or internal consistency checks test relationships between fields (dates, term, age) in the same record; such impossibilities are corrected before valuation.

t: When policies are grouped by valuation age, lives aged 40 to 44 next birthday would commonly be valued at a central age of
e: Grouping with a central age (mid-point of the band, here 42) keeps errors from averaging small and symmetrical, provided the group is reasonably homogeneous.

t: A net premium valuation of a policy with sum assured ₹4,00,000 uses A = 0.55, net premium 0.03 per ₹1 sum assured and ä = 9. The reserve is

Over the last three years, death claims occurring before the valuation date but intimated afterwards averaged ₹60 lakh per year. The in-force portfolio has grown and the actuary expects 10% more this year. The IBNR reserve should be about
e: IBNR = 60 lakh × 1.10 = ₹66 lakh, estimated from the past reporting-lag experience adjusted for growth.

t: Why may a prudent gross premium valuation ignore (or limit) the allowance for future lapses?
o: Allowing for lapses can reduce reserves, so prudence requires treating lapses only where they increase the liability
IRDAI requires a zero lapse rate for all plans
e: Where policy values are positive and exceed surrender values, lapse assumptions reduce reserves; a prudent basis includes lapses only when they make the liability larger (e.g. where guaranteed surrender values exceed the reserve).

t: A simple reversionary bonus of ₹45 per ₹1,000 sum assured is declared on a policy of ₹8,00,000. The bonus added for the year is
e: Bonus = 8,00,000 × 45/1,000 = ₹36,000, added as a reversionary (payable with the sum assured) addition.

t: Expense loadings in the premiums for the year amounted to ₹5 crore while actual expenses were ₹5.6 crore. The expense result for the year is
e: Expense surplus = loadings − actual expenses = 5.0 − 5.6 = −₹60 lakh, i.e. an expense strain that reduces the year's surplus.

t: A policy pays an annual premium of ₹10,000. Initial expenses are ₹4,000 and renewal expenses ₹500 per year; the fund earns 8% and mortality is ignored. The asset share at the end of the second year is approximately
In the early years of a regular-premium policy the asset share is usually below the net premium reserve because
o: interest earned is lower than assumed
actual initial expenses have been deducted in full from the asset share
e: The asset share charges the heavy first-year expenses as incurred, whereas the net premium reserve spreads expenses implicitly; the gap closes as the loadings in later premiums are received.

t: Since 1 April 2021, the standard fire policy for a dwelling in India is:
o: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bharat Griha Raksha for homes; Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (up to ₹5 crore) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha (₹5–50 crore) for enterprises.

t: A paid-up policy of ₹50,000 is surrendered. The office values the paid-up benefit at an assurance factor of 0.70 and deducts 5% from the result. The surrender value payable is
Surrender values are normally set somewhat below the policy reserve partly to guard against anti-selection. Here anti-selection means that
o: lives in poor health tend to surrender
agents sell only to the healthy
lives in good health are more likely to surrender, leaving heavier mortality in the remaining portfolio
e: Those who surrender tend to be the healthier lives (the impaired keep their cover), so the remaining group experiences heavier mortality; paying less than the full reserve offsets this.

t: A policyholder reduces the sum assured of an endowment policy from ₹5,00,000 to ₹3,00,000 with the same term. On equitable principles the reserve on the ₹2,00,000 released portion is
o: added to the bonus of the remaining policy
treated as a surrender of that portion (cash or paid-up benefit) and the premium reduced proportionately
e: A reduction is a partial surrender: the reserve on the reduced portion is applied for the policyholder's benefit and the future premium corresponds to the reduced sum assured.

t: A guaranteed annuity option in a deferred pension contract exposes the insurer chiefly to
o: a combination of falling interest rates and improving longevity
e: The guaranteed rate becomes valuable (costly to the insurer) when market interest rates fall and annuitants live longer than priced; both move the cost of the option against the office.

t: Under IRDAI norms, the minimum required solvency ratio (available solvency margin to required solvency margin) that a life insurer must maintain is
e: The control level of solvency is 150%, i.e. available solvency margin must be at least 1.5 times the required solvency margin at all times.

t: Which product builds up the largest reserve per ₹1 sum assured in the early policy years?
e: The shorter the endowment term, the larger the saving element in each premium and the faster the reserve must reach the sum assured, so a 10-year endowment accumulates reserves fastest; term assurance holds very little.

t: A term assurance quotes a lower office premium for non-smokers than for smokers. This differentiation is justified by
o: higher interest earned on their premiums
e: Premium differentiation must reflect expected cost; non-smokers show materially lighter mortality, so their risk premium is lower while expense and interest assumptions are the same.

t: A decreasing term assurance is most commonly used to
o: cover an outstanding housing loan that reduces over time
e: Because the sum assured falls each year in line with the loan balance outstanding, a decreasing term assurance matches a mortgage liability at a low premium.

t: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act 1938, a life insurance policy cannot be called in question on any ground after how many years from the date of issue, revival or rider addition, whichever is later?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The 2015 amendment made the three-year bar absolute: after three years no policy may be questioned on any ground, including fraud.

t: The select period in a mortality table is the period after which
o: the policy acquires a surrender value
the effect of medical selection on mortality is assumed to have worn off
e: Newly underwritten lives show lighter mortality than the general insured population; after the select period (e.g. 2–3 years) their mortality is assumed to merge into the ultimate rates.

t: Which statement about the net premium method is correct?
o: It is independent of the office premium actually charged
It always gives lower reserves than the gross premium method
It cannot be used for with-profits business
e: The net premium method computes its own net premium on the valuation basis and makes no explicit allowance for expenses; it is widely used for with-profits business and can give higher or lower reserves than a gross premium method depending on bases.

t: A reserve held to cover the effect of an epidemic or other adverse mortality shock is called a
e: A mortality fluctuation or catastrophe reserve is an additional reserve for random or extreme adverse deviations in mortality beyond the expected level.

t: The two principal tools by which a life insurer controls mortality risk are
o: underwriting at entry and reinsurance of large sums
e: Underwriting ensures premiums are charged according to the risk accepted, and reinsurance limits the financial effect of large individual claims on the fund.
